title: Area II review: Technical Subject Areas
intro: These questions mix the fourteen ASEL Tasks of Area II: human factors, scanning, runway incursions, aerodynamics, systems, performance, airspace, navigation, cross-country planning, regulations, endorsements, night and high-altitude operations. Many join two of them in one real instructing situation, the way an examiner would ask.

questions.q: Your learner smokes a pack a day. He plans his first night cross-country at 6,500 ft in an unpressurized trainer with no oxygen aboard, and says oxygen is a high-altitude topic that does not apply to him. How do you answer?
options: Smoking matters only for hypoxia at high altitude, but the AIM requires oxygen above 5,000 ft at night for anyone who smokes, so he needs a bottle aboard and a mask fitted before this trip
Oxygen is required by rule for every pilot above 5,000 ft at night, so he must fly lower or carry oxygen; his smoking does not affect night vision, only his tolerance for hypoxia above 12,500 ft
No rule requires it, but the AIM encourages oxygen above 5,000 ft at night, night vision fades measurably above 4,000 ft, and his smoking already costs about 20 percent of it at sea level

He is right: 91.211 starts above 12,500 ft cabin altitude, so altitude plays no part in his night vision at 6,500 ft, and smoking harms his lungs and heart but has no measurable effect on his eyes at night
questions.why: For optimum protection the AIM encourages supplemental oxygen above 10,000 ft by day and above 5,000 ft at night, while the rule only requires crew oxygen above 12,500 ft cabin altitude [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]] [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]. So the rule does not require it, but that is not the whole answer. Without oxygen, night vision declines measurably above 4,000 ft pressure altitude [[1:446|PHAK 17-24]], and the PHAK suggests pilots who fly at night strongly consider oxygen where the FAA does not require it [[1:449|PHAK 17-27]]. Smoking is the self-imposed stressor that most decreases night sensitivity: smokers lose 20 percent of night vision at sea level, equal to a physiological altitude of 5,000 ft [[1:447|PHAK 17-25]]. Saying the rule requires it at 5,000 ft confuses the recommendation with the regulation.

questions.q: Your learner made a scuba dive with no decompression stops that ended 14 hours ago. Tonight she wants to cruise at 9,500 ft MSL on a magnetic course of 060, well over 3,000 ft above the terrain. What altitude do you approve?
options: Any altitude she likes, because the dive wait times apply only to cabin altitude in pressurized airplanes, and 9,500 ft fits the odd-plus-500 rule
7,500 ft: 14 hours covers the 12-hour wait up to 8,000 ft, but above 8,000 ft needs 24 hours after any dive, and 7,500 fits the odd-plus-500 rule for 060
8,000 ft exactly, because the 12-hour dive limit runs up to 8,000 ft and level flight at the limit itself is allowed on any course
9,500 ft, because more than 12 hours have passed since a dive without decompression stops, and 9,500 ft fits the odd-thousand-plus-500 rule for a course of 060
questions.why: The AIM recommends at least 12 hours after a dive without decompression stops before flying up to 8,000 ft, and at least 24 hours after any dive before flying above 8,000 ft. These are actual altitudes above MSL, not cabin altitudes [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]], so 9,500 ft is out tonight and the pressurized-only idea is wrong. More than 3,000 ft above the surface on a magnetic course of 0 through 179, the VFR cruising altitude is an odd thousand plus 500 [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159(a)(1)]], so 7,500 ft works. A level cruise at exactly 8,000 ft is not a VFR cruising altitude for that course.

questions.q: To show why early detection matters, you give your learner this problem: you fly at 110 knots and an airplane comes head-on at 140 knots. Using the 12.5 seconds in AC 90-48E Table 1 from first seeing it until your airplane begins to move, how much closer do the two airplanes get?
options: About 0.3 NM
About 0.9 NM
About 0.1 NM
About 4 NM
questions.why: The closure rate is 110 + 140 = 250 knots. In 12.5 seconds that is 250 x 12.5 / 3,600 = 0.87 NM, about 0.9 NM, before the airplane even starts to move [[16:6|AC 90-48E Table 1]]. Add the 1 to 2 seconds the eyes need to refocus from the panel, and it is about 1 NM [[16:5|AC 90-48E 8.1.4]]. About 0.3 NM counts only the 4-second decision, and 4 NM is a full minute of closure. High closure rates limit the time for detection, decision and evasive action [[24:31|AFH 1-10]], which is why the scan must find traffic early.

questions.q: Your practice area lies under the outer shelf of a Class C, near a nontowered airport. The tablet's ADS-B traffic page is empty, and your learner wants to skip the clearing turns before steep turns to save time. What do you teach?
options: The AIM warns of VFR aircraft with no transponder or ADS-B under the shelf, and those never show on ADS-B In; an empty screen proves nothing, so clear every time
Ask approach for traffic advisories instead, since radar service takes over the see and avoid duty under a Class C shelf once she has radar contact
Skipping them is fine when the display has a traffic alert feature, because ADS-B In shows every aircraft under the Class C shelf, transponder or not, in real time
Clearing turns are needed only within 5 NM of an airport, so out under the shelf of the Class C one careful look ahead before each steep turn is enough for safety
questions.why: The AIM warns that pilots below the base of the 5 to 10 mile Class C shelf may meet VFR aircraft with no transponder or ADS-B [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4]], and aircraft without ADS-B Out or a transponder will not be visible on an ADS-B In display [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]]. Traffic equipment does not relieve the pilot's duty to see and avoid [[16:14|AC 90-48E 15]], and radar traffic information does not relieve continual vigilance either [[33:214|AIM 4-1-15]]. The AFH tells the instructor to teach an effective clearing procedure, insist on it, and have the learner clear before all turns and every training maneuver [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

questions.q: Your student's first solo cross-country goes to a busy towered airport with two hot spots, with a nontowered alternate picked along the route. She has printed only the destination's airport diagram. What does AC 91-73B recommend you require?
options: Current airport diagrams for the departure, arrival and alternate airports, used and understood, with each hot spot briefed from its description on the Hot Spot page in the front of the TPP
Only the destination diagram, because nontowered airports have no taxi clearances
No diagram at the alternate, since she can ask for progressive taxi anywhere
Any diagram she already owns, whatever its date, for the nontowered alternate
questions.why: AC 91-73B highly recommends that CFIs instruct students in the meaning and use of airport diagrams, and recommends that CFIs require students to have and use current diagrams for departure, arrival and alternate airports [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2) NOTE]]. A hot spot is a brown circle or ellipse on the diagram leadered to a number that matches a description on the Hot Spot page in the front of the TPP [[2:124|Chart Users' Guide, Hot Spots]]. The PHAK also tells pilots to check the charts for airports along or near the route before any cross-country [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]], so the alternate is part of the plan, not an afterthought. An old diagram fails the 'current' test.

questions.q: After landing at a towered airport, your student raises the flaps and switches to ground while still rolling on the runway. He says, "That's what you always do." What is the right correction?
options: It is fine as long as he calls the flap change out loud and keeps the airplane on centerline, since a callout makes any action on the rollout safe, and switching to ground early helps the tower
Nothing nonessential (flaps, trim, frequency) until the whole airplane, tail included, is past the hold markings; stay with tower until told to change, and model it, since learners copy you

Only the flap change is wrong: the frequency change is the pilot's choice, and switching to ground while still rolling is normal practice that towers expect at busy airports, so he can keep that habit
Switch to ground as soon as the turn off the runway starts, to save the tower's time, and raise the flaps once below taxi speed; the hold markings matter only for airplanes entering the runway
questions.why: AC 91-73B says nonessential communications and actions, such as changing frequencies and repositioning flaps and trim, should not start until clear of all runways, and that the entire aircraft, including the tail, must cross the landing runway's hold short line [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(11)]] [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(13)]]. A pilot who just landed should not change from tower to ground until the controller directs it [[33:258|AIM 4-3-14]]. The student's last sentence is the real lesson: learners treat the instructor as a role model, and safety practices the instructor describes but does not demonstrate mean little [[25:164|AIH 8-6]].

questions.q: In slow flight at high power, your learner says, "Something is wrong. The controls are mushy and the nose keeps swinging left with the wings level." How do you explain it?
options: Normal: at low airspeed the controls feel soft and need larger inputs, and torque, slipstream and P-factor give a strong left yaw that needs more right rudder near the stall
Gyroscopic precession is pulling the nose left at the high pitch attitude; hold left aileron against it and the swing will stop by itself once the airspeed and pitch settle down
It is adverse yaw only, from holding aileron; neutralize the ailerons and the yaw will stop, and the soft controls mean the trim is set too far nose-up
It is a rigging fault: mushy controls and a yaw with the wings level are never normal in slow flight, so return and have the airplane inspected
questions.why: At low airspeeds the controls usually feel soft and sluggish and the airplane responds slowly; at higher airspeeds they get firm and quick [[1:151|PHAK 6-3]]. In slow flight the elevator is less responsive and larger movements are needed, and torque, slipstream effect and P-factor may produce a strong left yaw that needs right rudder, more of it the closer the airplane is to the 1G stall [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. P-factor comes from the descending blade taking a bigger bite at high angle of attack [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]]. Gyroscopic precession shows up with pitch changes, mostly raising the tail of a tailwheel airplane, and adverse yaw comes from aileron deflection, not from wings-level flight.

questions.q: On a dual flight before solo, your student is cleared to land behind a regional jet that is departing the same runway. He plans to touch down far down the runway "to be past its wake." What do you teach?
options: He is right: land beyond the jet's rotation point, since a departing jet leaves its strongest wake on the first part of the runway
Land well before the jet's rotation point, since its vortices start at rotation; avoiding the wake is his job, caution or not
Land at the normal point, since jets make vortices only on approach and landing, never during the takeoff roll or climb
Wait 2 minutes before landing, because that interval covers every departure of a larger aircraft from the same runway
questions.why: An aircraft generates vortices from the moment it rotates on takeoff to touchdown, so note the rotation point of the preceding aircraft [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]]. Landing behind a departing larger aircraft on the same runway, note its rotation point and land well prior to it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. Landing past it puts the airplane in the wake. The 2-minute interval is for takeoffs or landings after a larger aircraft's low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]], not this case. Whether or not ATC gives a caution, the pilot is expected to adjust the flight path to avoid wake encounters [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

questions.q: On a cross-country in a retractable trainer, the right main gear will not extend by the normal or the POH alternate method. You have 2 hours of fuel, and a towered airport with crash and rescue equipment is 25 minutes away. What does the AFH have you plan?
options: Go to the airport with crash and rescue, ask for equipment to stand by, and burn off fuel, mostly from the right tanks, so the right wing touches down as late as possible
Land now at the nearest grass strip with the fuel still aboard, because an unimproved surface always does less damage than a hard runway and burning fuel changes nothing about the landing
Go to the towered airport but burn fuel only from the left tanks, so the left main carries less weight and the right wing stays up longer on the rollout
Keep all the fuel for options and fly to the airport with crash and rescue, but ask for nothing, since requesting emergency equipment turns it into an NTSB accident
questions.why: Once a gear leg will not respond to the normal or alternate AFM/POH methods, a gear-up landing is considered inevitable. Select an airport with crash and rescue facilities if possible, and do not hesitate to ask for emergency equipment to stand by. A smooth, hard runway usually causes less damage than a rough grass strip, although it can make sparks. Consider burning off excess fuel to reduce landing speed and fire potential, and if only one main leg has failed, use as much fuel as practicable from that side so the unsupported wing contacts the surface as late as possible [[24:361|AFH 18-12]]. Burning from the good side does the opposite.

questions.q: Preflighting for a cross-country, your learner reads both fuel gauges at FULL and does not look in the tanks. Her plan is to watch the gauges and land when they show low. What do you teach?
options: A visual check is needed only for the first flight of the day; after that the gauges are reliable, so her plan to land when they show low meets 91.151 by itself
Plan the fuel by distance at true airspeed, since wind does not change fuel burned, then land when the gauges show low or the planned distance is flown
Gauges are certified accurate across the whole scale, so her plan works as long as she lands when either gauge first shows low, which keeps the 30-minute day reserve 91.151 requires on every flight
Gauges need be accurate only at empty, so check the tanks visually; plan fuel by time from groundspeed with the 91.151 reserve, and land before that time runs out or the gauge shows low
questions.why: Certification requires fuel gauges to be accurate only when they read empty, so the pilot should not depend on them alone and should visually check each tank on preflight and compare it with the gauge [[1:186|PHAK 7-26]]. Fuel needed is flight time from groundspeed times the burn rate, because burn stays about the same at a given TAS, plus an adequate reserve, and the pilot should plan to be on the ground before the computed fuel time is used up or before the gauge shows low [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. The rule sets the minimum: enough to reach the first point of intended landing and fly 30 minutes by day or 45 at night [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151]].

questions.q: Your learner's airplane weighs 3,030 lb at takeoff, and its maximum landing weight is 2,950 lb. It burns 12 GPH of avgas. What minimum flight time goes on her plan before landing, and what should she know if an emergency forces her down sooner?
options: About 13 minutes; nothing special after an early landing
No minimum, since maximum landing weight applies only to transport airplanes
About 67 minutes; an earlier emergency landing uses structural margin that is not fully available, so an overweight landing inspection may be advisable
About 40 minutes; landing overweight is never allowed, even in an emergency
questions.why: She must burn 3,030 - 2,950 = 80 lb. At 6 lb per gallon [[1:251|PHAK 10-7]] that is 13.3 gallons, and at 12 GPH that is 1.11 hours, about 67 minutes. The W&B Handbook works the same kind of case, where an airplane loaded properly for takeoff must burn off fuel before it can land [[22:54|W&B 5-6]]. A maximum landing weight is a limitation that calls for planning the fuel burn; in an emergency needing an immediate landing, the pilot should recognize that the designed structural margins are not fully available, and an overweight landing inspection may be advisable [[24:263|AFH 13-14]]. About 13 is the gallons, not the minutes.

questions.q: A learner's loaded airplane weighs 2,400 lb with the CG at 47.5 inches, behind the 47.0-inch aft limit. She will move baggage from the aft compartment (arm 95) to the empty rear seat (arm 73). You first ask which way the CG will move. Then: what is the least weight she must move?
options: About 12 lb
About 25 lb
About 55 lb
About 109 lb
questions.why: Weight to shift = total weight x change in CG / distance shifted [[22:24|W&B 2-4]]. The CG must move 47.5 - 47.0 = 0.5 inch over a shift of 95 - 73 = 22 inches: 2,400 x 0.5 / 22 = 54.5 lb, so at least about 55 lb. About 109 lb is what a 1-inch change would need. Asking first which way the CG moves follows the PHAK's advice to decide that mentally: moving weight forward, the change is subtracted from the old CG [[1:255|PHAK 10-11]]. It also catches a learner who would move the bag the wrong way.

questions.q: On flight following, approach says "radar contact," and later gives your learner a heading toward the solid blue line of a Class B. She says, "We're radar contact and on a vector, so we're cleared in." What do you teach?
options: She is right: radar contact plus a vector toward the Class B counts as a clearance, because ATC would never point a VFR airplane at airspace it may not enter without first clearing her
Radar contact means only that she is identified for flight following; Class B needs a clearance before entry in any weather, and a vector never authorizes breaking a rule
She may enter if she stays clear of clouds, since that is the Class B VFR cloud rule, and radar contact already satisfies the two-way radio requirement
She may enter once ATC assigns a discrete squawk, since a discrete code is the controller's way of clearing a VFR aircraft into Class B airspace
questions.why: "Radar contact" tells a pilot the aircraft is identified and radar flight following will be provided until service ends [[34:401|AIM PCG R-2]]. It is not a clearance. The operator must receive an ATC clearance before operating in Class B [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(a)(1)]], and the AIM says that is so regardless of weather [[33:179|AIM 3-2-3]]. Radar navigational guidance to a VFR pilot is advisory and does not authorize violating the regulations [[33:217|AIM 4-1-17]]. Clear of clouds is the Class B cloud rule once inside, and a squawk code is not a clearance either.

questions.q: Your student plans 11,500 ft MSL on a magnetic course of 075 over terrain near 1,000 ft MSL. The trainer has a Mode C transponder but no ADS-B Out. What is wrong with the plan?
options: Oxygen is required for the whole time above 10,000 ft, so plan 9,500 ft; ADS-B Out matters only inside the Mode C veil around a Class B airport
ADS-B Out is required in Class E at and above 10,000 ft MSL in the 48 states, except at or below 2,500 ft AGL, and the chart does not show it; plan 9,500 ft
Nothing: 11,500 ft fits the eastbound rule, and a Mode C transponder is all that is needed below 18,000 ft MSL, since ADS-B Out is required only inside Class A airspace
Eastbound needs even thousands plus 500, so 10,500 ft, and Mode C alone meets the equipment rule at any altitude below 18,000 ft MSL
questions.why: Both an altitude-reporting transponder and ADS-B Out are required at and above 10,000 ft MSL over the 48 contiguous states and DC, excluding airspace at and below 2,500 ft above the surface [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(5)(i)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(4)]]. At 11,500 ft over 1,000 ft terrain the airplane is 10,500 ft above the surface, so the rule applies. The Chart Users' Guide says this en route requirement is not depicted [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p.17]], which is why students miss it. For a magnetic course of 0 to 179, odd thousands plus 500 is correct [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159(a)(1)]], so 9,500 ft works. Oxygen is not required until above 12,500 ft cabin altitude [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].

questions.q: Diverting, your student finds the alternate airport sits on the 060 radial of a VOR, 12 NM out. You are now right over that VOR. How should she set the OBS and flag to track to the airport with normal, not reversed, needle sensing?
options: OBS 240 with a TO indication
OBS 240 with a FROM indication
OBS 060 with a TO indication
OBS 060 with a FROM indication
questions.why: The heading of a VOR radial is outbound from the station [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]], so the airport lies along course 060 away from the VOR. With FROM showing, the course set is followed away from the station [[1:411|PHAK 16-24]]. Flying away from the station with 240 and TO set gives reverse sensing: when flying FROM, fly the selected course with a FROM indication, or the needle acts backward [[1:413|PHAK 16-26]]. Once on the 060 radial the receiver cannot show TO with 060 set, and 240 FROM belongs to the other side of the station. Have the student say the position first, then set the OBS.

questions.q: For his first solo cross-country, your student plans to navigate only by a hand-held GPS with its antenna on a suction cup on the side window. What do you teach before you sign his endorsement?
options: Fine: a hand-held unit's RAIM will warn him of any satellite or antenna problem, so with a current database the GPS can safely be his only means of navigation on this first solo cross-country
Hand-helds have no RAIM alerting and a cabin antenna can lose satellites with no warning, so GPS must be integrated with pilotage and dead reckoning, which 61.93 training covers
With a current database a hand-held may be his only means of navigation, since the AIM's only requirement for VFR GPS use is an up-to-date database and a charged battery
Hand-held GPS is banned by regulation for VFR navigation, so he must remove it and fly by pilotage, dead reckoning and the VOR only
questions.why: VFR panel-mount and hand-held receivers have no RAIM alerting, and suction-cup antennas inside the cabin rarely see all satellites, so signal loss plus no RAIM can give a wrong position with no warning [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]]. VFR pilots should never rely solely on one system; GPS must be integrated with other navigation, pilotage and dead reckoning [[1:419|PHAK 16-32]]. Hand-held use for VFR is not limited by regulation [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]], so a ban is wrong. Before a solo cross-country the student must have training in the use of charts for VFR navigation using pilotage and dead reckoning with the aid of a magnetic compass [[60:281|14 CFR 61.93(e)]].

questions.q: Your private pilot learner gets airsick on bumpy days and plans to take an over-the-counter motion sickness pill before tomorrow's cross-country as PIC. What do you teach?
options: Fine if she takes it at least 8 hours before departure, since the 8-hour bottle-to-throttle rule for alcohol applies to every medication the same way, prescription or not
Fine, since over-the-counter medicines are exempt from 91.17, which covers only prescription drugs and alcohol, so she can take the pill an hour before departure and fly the whole trip as usual
Airsickness shows she is not suited to flying, so she should stop training rather than take any medicine for it
Those pills help passengers but are not advised for pilots since they cause drowsiness, and 91.17 bars flying on any drug that impairs faculties; airsickness says nothing about her ability
questions.why: Medications like Dramamine can prevent airsickness in passengers but are not recommended while flying because they can cause drowsiness and other problems, and airsickness is no reflection on one's ability as a pilot [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. Motion sickness agents have side effects that may impair judgment, memory, alertness and coordination [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]], and 91.17 bars acting as a crewmember while using any drug that affects the person's faculties in any way contrary to safety [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17]]. The 8-hour rule is for alcohol, and nothing exempts over-the-counter drugs.

questions.q: Your solo student's VFR flight plan shows an ETA of 1430Z at a towered airport. She lands at 1420Z, ties down and goes to lunch, sure the tower closed her plan. If nobody closes it, when do search and rescue procedures start?
options: 1630Z, two hours after the ETA
Never; the tower closed it when she landed
1530Z, one hour after the ETA
1500Z, half an hour after the ETA, because towers do not close VFR flight plans; she must close it with Flight Service or ask an ATC facility to relay it
questions.why: The pilot is responsible for canceling the plan, with the nearest FSS or through any ATC facility as a relay. Control towers do not automatically close VFR flight plans, and if the pilot fails to report or cancel within 1/2 hour after the ETA, search and rescue procedures start [[60:464|14 CFR 91.153(b)]] [[33:339|AIM 5-1-14]]. So 1430Z + 0:30 = 1500Z. Two hours is how long an unactivated proposal is normally kept, a different rule [[33:331|AIM 5-1-5]].

questions.q: Your learner says AC 91-78A is only an advisory circular, so flying VFR with her tablet's expired charts breaks no rule as long as the paper charts stay home. How do you teach it?
options: She is right: advisory circulars never matter to a part 91 pilot, and no regulation says anything about information currency on a VFR flight
She is wrong because every advisory circular becomes binding on the public as soon as the FAA posts it on its website, AC 91-78A included
An AC binds only when a rule incorporates it, but 91.103 has the PIC learn all available information, and expired charts are not all of it
She is wrong because AC 91-78A is incorporated by reference into 91.103, which turns every one of its EFB recommendations into a binding rule for every pilot
questions.why: The AIM says an AC's contents are not binding on the public unless incorporated into a regulation by reference [[33:54|AIM Code of Federal Regulations and Advisory Circulars]], so 'it is only an AC' is half right. But 91.103 requires each PIC, before beginning a flight, to become familiar with all available information concerning that flight [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]], and the Chart Users' Guide tells pilots to use current editions and discard obsolete ones [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide 6]]. AC 91-78A itself lets an EFB replace paper only when its information is current and valid, as verified by the pilot [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.1]]. Nothing makes the AC itself a rule, so the incorporation answer is wrong too.

questions.q: A learner reads AIM 4-4-6 and says night special VFR is legal for any instrument-rated pilot in an IFR-equipped airplane. How do you teach it?
options: The AIM wording is binding because it is the FAA's official guide to ATC procedures, so any instrument-rated pilot in an IFR-equipped airplane may fly night special VFR anywhere
Night special VFR is prohibited for every fixed-wing pilot, whatever the rating or equipment, because 91.157 allows it only from sunrise to sunset
The rule only requires the airplane to be IFR-equipped under 91.205(d); the pilot needs no instrument rating or currency for night special VFR
The AIM is not regulatory, so read the rule: 91.157 allows night fixed-wing SVFR only if the pilot meets part 61 instrument requirements and the airplane meets 91.205(d)
questions.why: The AIM says of itself that it is not regulatory; it shows techniques and procedures that may be required by other regulations [[33:53|AIM Flight Information Publication Policy]]. AIM 4-4-6 says fixed-wing night SVFR needs an instrument-rated pilot and an IFR-equipped aircraft [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]], but the rule says between sunrise and sunset unless the person meets the applicable part 61 requirements for instrument flight and the aircraft is equipped as required in 91.205(d) [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)(4)]]. Teach the CFR wording, and use the difference to show the learner why the rule comes first and the guidance second.

questions.q: Your student holds a current solo endorsement and wants to fly solo to a nontowered field 18 NM away to practice landings. You have never flown there with her. What is required?
options: Nothing extra, since it is within 25 NM and her current solo endorsement already covers takeoffs and landings at any airport inside that distance
The full solo cross-country endorsements of 61.93(c), since any landing away from the home airport counts as a solo cross-country, plus a new per-flight endorsement each and every time she goes there
A repeated solo cross-country endorsement for flights within 50 NM, which you can sign after one dual flight to the airport, without flying the route in both directions with her
Training at that airport, with flight both ways over the route, pattern entry and exit, and takeoffs and landings; then, if proficient, an endorsement for solo landings there with any conditions
questions.why: 61.93(b)(1) allows solo flights to another airport within 25 NM of where the student normally trains, for the purpose of practicing takeoffs and landings, only after an authorized instructor has given flight training at that airport, including both directions over the route, entering and exiting the pattern, and takeoffs and landings there. The instructor who gave the training endorses the logbook, the student holds a 61.87 solo endorsement, and the instructor has found her proficient [[60:280|14 CFR 61.93(b)(1)]]. AC 61-65K sample A.8 states that and leaves room for conditions [[12:41|AC 61-65K A.8]]. The 50 NM repeated cross-country endorsement is a separate case under 61.93(b)(2) [[60:280|14 CFR 61.93(b)(2)]].

questions.q: A private pilot's last flight review endorsement is dated March 10, 2025, and he has done nothing since that would replace it. Through what date may he act as PIC?
options: March 10, 2027
February 28, 2027
March 31, 2027
April 30, 2027
questions.why: No person may act as PIC unless, since the beginning of the 24th calendar month before the month in which the pilot acts as PIC, the pilot has completed a flight review [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]]. For a flight in March 2027, the 24th calendar month before is March 2025, and the review on March 10 falls after the beginning of that month, so he is good all of March 2027. For April 2027 the period starts April 1, 2025, and the review is too old. March 10, 2027 is the common misreading: the rule counts calendar months, not days, so read it to the end. The A.69 endorsement records the date the review was completed [[12:53|AC 61-65K A.69]].

questions.q: Unpressurized, by day, your commercial learner will fly as PIC, the only required crewmember, at 13,500 ft cabin altitude for 75 minutes on a magnetic course of 110. A private pilot friend rides in the right seat as a passenger. What does 91.211 require, and what do you recommend?
options: The PIC must use oxygen for 45 minutes and the friend needs none by rule; the FAA recommends oxygen for both whenever above 10,000 ft by day
Both pilots must use oxygen for all 75 minutes, because both are pilots
The PIC needs 75 minutes and the friend 45 minutes
No one needs oxygen, because 13,500 ft is below 14,000 ft
questions.why: Above 12,500 ft up to and including 14,000 ft cabin altitude, the required minimum flight crew must use oxygen for the part of the flight there of more than 30 minutes: 75 - 30 = 45 minutes. Occupants must be provided oxygen only above 15,000 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]. The friend is not required crew, so a pilot certificate does not make him one. The FAA recommends oxygen on any unpressurized flight to or above 10,000 ft by day [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7]], so plan for both. 13,500 ft also fits the VFR cruising rule for this course: odd thousands plus 500 [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159(a)(1)]].

questions.q: Your learner's pressurized single will cruise at FL 270 with three passengers. She plans to skip the oxygen part of the passenger briefing because the masks will drop automatically, as on an airliner. What do you teach?
options: Automatic masks are a Part 25 feature; her passengers may have to don their own, and above FL 250 each needs a 10-minute supply, so brief it
She is right: every pressurized airplane drops its passenger masks automatically before the cabin reaches 15,000 ft, so no oxygen briefing is needed at all
Above FL 250 only the required crew must have oxygen, so the passengers need neither a mask briefing nor any oxygen supply of their own
Brief it only after a decompression happens, since 91.211 lets the pilot hand masks to the passengers during the emergency descent instead
questions.why: Pressurized aircraft meeting the more stringent requirements of part 25 have automatic passenger oxygen mask-dispensing devices that activate before the cabin exceeds 15,000 ft [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9]]. The AC names no such device for smaller airplanes, so her passengers may have to find and don their own masks, which makes the briefing part of the decompression response. Above FL 250 in a pressurized aircraft, at least a 10-minute supply of supplemental oxygen must be available for each occupant for a descent after a loss of cabin pressurization [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]], so the rule covers passengers too.

questions.q: On a night cross-country, the destination's runway lights take on a faint halo as you descend. Your learner continues, enters a shallow fog layer on short final and abruptly steepens the descent. What do you teach?
options: Fog makes the runway look farther away than it is, so pushing over to get down sooner was right; the halo was only glare from a dirty windshield, which the landing light would fix
Nothing unusual happened: fog causes no illusion of its own, and a halo simply shows the runway lights were set to high intensity for the approach
The halo pointed to ground fog, and entering fog can create an illusion of pitching up, so pilots steepen the approach, often abruptly; brief it and fly the PAPI and altimeter
Fog creates an illusion of being too low, so the learner should have climbed; a halo around runway lights means the lights are on their highest setting
questions.why: A halo or glow around lights on the ground indicates ground fog, and further flight in the same direction calls for caution [[24:226|AFH 11-9]]. Penetration of fog can create the illusion of pitching up, and the pilot who does not recognize it will steepen the approach, often quite abruptly [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5]]. Greater apparent distance is the haze illusion, not the fog one [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5]]. The defenses are to anticipate illusions at unfamiliar airports at night, refer to the altimeter often and use the VASI or PAPI [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]] [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].
